synopsis: Across the booklet, HIL places a real or representative ECU and its I/O against a real-time simulated plant to establish timing, communications, diagnostics, fault response and fail-to-safe behavior; SIL cannot prove the final ECU’s timing, processor or I/O faults [f533, f5279, f13350, f5269]. Expanding the real test boundary from software to ECU, sensor and machine captures more failure modes but reduces speed, scalability and controllability, while ECU-level injection still leaves the sensor front end unproven [f5227, f12970]. HIL requires hard real time, and realistic sensor values alone are insufficient: synchronization, network delays, ECU scheduling and actuator latency can defeat braking, while an offline-accurate renderer may fail deterministic ECU timing [f13418, f5092, f8923]. Most infrastructure can be developed before final hardware arrives using established interfaces and surrogate controllers, but a production-relevant ISO/TS 21815-2 HIL bench is only a possible mid-2027 target and should not become critical-path work unless ECU, bus and actuator interfaces stabilize early [f5568, f5587, f5588, f857]. Sensor stimulation is recommended for final sensor/ECU regression, timing tests and supplier-independent characterization, but injection remains sensor- and ECU-specific and bidirectional sensor–ECU behavior remains an open interface issue [f4500, f8641, f5093]. Brake-request timing and fault behavior require evidence separate from sensor realism; one mining-regime example specifies disconnection detection within 500 ms and a machine reply within 50 ms, rather than establishing universal thresholds [f12975, f12969].
